Association Between Urban Informality and Maternal Mortality

Diego Pajarito Grajales

2026-09-02

Introduction

This analysis evaluates whether mortality rates differ across grid cells classified as having low, medium, or high urban informality. Population counts are used as an offset so that estimated effects represent differences in mortality rates rather than differences in population size.

Models:

  1. Poisson
  2. Negative Binomial

Data

Inputs:

Data inputs are the model results from IDEAMAPS (deprivation), mortality cases from Kassep and population (WorlPOP women of childbearing age.

mortality_json <- "./data/maternaldeaths.geojson"
grid_gpkg <- "./data/model-output-classification.gpkg"
grid_layer <- "deprivation-classification"
pop_gpkg <- "./data/pop-grid-kano-centroids.gpkg"
pop_layer <- "pop-grid-kano-centroids"

Load Mortality Cases

This is a JSON file recording maternal mortality cases from KASSEP

## Cases loaded. Rows: 78

Load EmOC Deprivation Grid

This is GeoPackage has the cells classified by EmOC access deprivation. There are two classifications applied to the EmOC access deprivation:

One including the three categories and a second one where Medium and High are conflated to reduce the classification to two categories.

## Deprivation loaded. Cells: 167239

Load women of childbearing age population to the Grid

This Geopackage has cells with the estimate number of women of childbearing age. Such values are the population values used in the model. The values are transferred by applying and spatial join operation. Since the final values are the result of estimates based on the presence of building footprints, the following columns are used:

  • pop: estimated number of women of childbearing age in the cell
  • pop_grid_pop: estimated population from the 1km x 1km grid cell (WorlPOP)
  • bcount: number of building footprints used to distribute population (1km -> 100m)
## Population loaded. Cells: 167260

Data Preparation

Preparation tasks include operations such as - Project Layers to Common CRS

  • Assign and count Mortality Cases to Grid Cells

Analysis data set

To prepare the analysis data set, it was required to consider that the overall aim is to compare how mortality rates (mortality cases within the population) change, or not change, accross the different EmOC acces deprivation categories.

For this, the dataset should i) exclude gridcells where there’s no population of women of child bearing age and ii) consider areas with and withouth recorded cases of maternal mortality

analysis_df <- grid %>%
  dplyr::filter(pop>0) %>% 
  left_join(case_counts, by = "grid_id") %>% 
  mutate(
    deaths = ifelse(is.na(deaths), 0, deaths)
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  dplyr::select(Accessibility_Index_Standard, informality_class, informality_class_mh, pop, deaths)

Model fitting

Step 1: Poisson Model without adjusting by population

Model fit for the three deprivation categories

This model serves as an initial exploration of the possible relationship between EmOC access deprivation and the count of mortality cases. However, the results are not optimal due to the lack of adjustment by population.

One of the drawbacks of not accounting for population size is that larger cells may naturally have more deaths simply because more people live there.

This model assumes H0: Beta = 0, Or equivalent to IRR = 0 A key to interpret the model is the IRR (effect size) and the confidence interval.

Below an example of how this could be interpreted:

IRR = 1.5 for Medium → medium informality cells have 50% more deaths than low informality cells. IRR = 2.0 for High → high informality cells have twice as many deaths as low informality cells.

poisson_unadjusted <- glm(
  deaths ~ informality_class,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = analysis_df
)
#summary(poisson_unadjusted)

# Extract coefficients
results <- tidy(
 poisson_unadjusted,
 exponentiate = TRUE,
 conf.int = TRUE,
)
# Keep only deprivation effects
results <- results %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
  term = gsub("informality_class", "", term)
)

results
## # A tibble: 2 × 7
##   term   estimate std.error statistic p.value conf.low conf.high

## 2 High       1.32     0.629     0.444   0.657    0.441      5.69

Step 2: Negative Binomial Model

The negative binomial model includes control by the population, in this case, of women of childbearing age. This compares the mortality rates between grid cells in the different categories of EmOC access deprivation. This model allows to describe how much higher (or lower) is mortality in other categories compared with low-deprivation cells.

The model considers facts related to maternal health such as death cases being rare events, unevenly distributed and often clustered spatially that leave many grid cells with ceros.

This model assumes H0: Beta = 0, Or equivalent to IRR = 0 A key to interpret the model is the IRR (effect size) and the 95% confidence interval.

Model fit for the three deprivation categories

nb_model <- glm.nb(
 deaths ~ informality_class + offset(log(pop)),
 data = analysis_df
)

summary(nb_model)

Step 3: Comparing Binomial GLM vs Poisson GLM

There are some factors that serve to decide which models are more adequate for the analysis. The comparison uses overdispertion, AIC and

Estimating a Poisson GLM model controlled by population

pois_model <- glm(
  deaths ~ informality_class +
  offset(log(pop)),
  family = poisson(),
  data = analysis_df
)

# Extract coefficients
results <- tidy(
 pois_model,
 exponentiate = TRUE,
 conf.int = TRUE,
)
# Keep only deprivation effects
results <- results %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
  term = gsub("informality_class_mh", "", term)
)

results

Over dispersion

Estimating

deviance(poisson_model) / df.residual(poisson_model)

sum(residuals(poisson_model, type=“pearson”)^2) / df.residual(poisson_model)

Ratio Value Interpretation - aprox 1 Poisson assumption reasonable - 1.5 - 2 Mild overdispersion - > 2 Substantial overdispersion - > 4 Strong overdispersion

for mortality data in grids, values above 2 are very common

rat_disp_v1 <- deviance(pois_model) / df.residual(pois_model)

rat_disp_v2 <- sum(residuals(pois_model, type="pearson")^2) /
  df.residual(pois_model)

data.frame(c("Deviance/Residual ", "sum(res--pearson)^2/residual "), c(rat_disp_v1, rat_disp_v2))
##   c..Deviance.Residual.....sum.res..pearson..2.residual...
## 1                                       Deviance/Residual 
## 2                            sum(res--pearson)^2/residual 
##   c.rat_disp_v1..rat_disp_v2.
## 1                 0.006543424
## 2                 1.581639336

AIC Values comparison

For this comparison, the two models will provide AIC values with the lower AIC values indicates the preferred model. The following are indications to support the decision

ΔAIC Interpretation - < 2 Models essentially equivalent - 2 - 4 Weak support for lower AIC model - 4 - 10 Moderate support - > 10 Strong support

AIC(pois_model, nb_model)
##            df      AIC
## pois_model  3 486.2700
## nb_model    4 510.1228

Step 3: Aggregating grid cells into 1km grid size

Having 100m grid cells makes the case of having thousands of cero values for mortality. Looking for an option to reduce this proportion, we tried to aggregate the cells. Since the model uses the 1km grid from WorldPOP

The process group the cells based on the unique value for the estimated population “pop_grid_pop”, dissolves the geometries and estimate new values for the accessibility index (avg), building count, and deprivation category (mode)

get_mode <- function(x) {
  ux <- unique(x)
  ux[which.max(tabulate(match(x, ux)))]
}

grid1k <- grid %>%
  group_by(pop_grid_pop) %>%
  summarise(
    bcount = sum(bcount, na.rm = TRUE),
    grid_count = n(),
    Accessibility_Index_avg = mean(
      Accessibility_Index_Standard,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    informality_mode = get_mode(result),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  rename(pop = pop_grid_pop)

grid1k <- tibble::rowid_to_column(grid1k, "id")

Estimating the new accessibility index

The index is estimated in two ways, one is the use of established thresholds to the newly averaged index and the second comes form the mode value.

Classify the accessibility into three categories based on the standardized Accessibility Index: 0 for High accessibility, 1 for Medium accessibility, and 2 for Low accessibility. The thresholds for classification are set at 0.005 and 0.02, which can be adjusted based on the distribution of the Accessibility Index in the dataset.

The thresholds used for the 100m grid cell are applied to the aggregated cells as: High: Value 2. Accessibility index (0.02 - 1) Medium: Value 1. Accessibility index (0.005 - 0.02) Low: Value 0. Accessibility index (0 - 0.005)

## Deprivation processed Cells: 2099

Negative Binomial Model using the 1k grid

The negative binomial model includes control by the population, in this case, of women of childbearing age. This compares the mortality rates between grid cells in the different categories of EmOC access deprivation. This model allows to describe how much higher (or lower) is mortality in other categories compared with low-deprivation cells.

The model considers facts related to maternal health such as death cases being rare events, unevenly distributed and often clustered spatially that leave many grid cells with ceros.

This model assumes H0: Beta = 0, Or equivalent to IRR = 0 A key to interpret the model is the IRR (effect size) and the 95% confidence interval.

Model fit for the three deprivation categories

nb_model_1k <- glm.nb(
 deaths ~ informality_class + offset(log(pop)),
 data = analysis_1k
)
